city.caveat: This is the official city record as kept, without adjustments. It joins several observing sites over the years, and a move, a new instrument or the city growing around a station can shift readings (city growth mostly warms nights); NOAA's adjusted climate datasets correct for these. Treat any single number as approximate.

text.lede: Yesterday's high of 49°F was typical for November 13.
text.p_yest: The high of 49°F was typical for November 13. The normal high for the date is 55°F, and the record is 74°F (1931). The low of 39°F was typical for November 13.
text.t_rec: Record highs keep coming. Record lows have nearly stopped.
text.p_rec: If Newark's climate weren't changing, every year would have the same chance of holding a daily record. Since 2000, Newark has set 6 standing record lows, far fewer than the 55 that chance alone would give, and 112 record highs, far more than the 55 that chance alone would give. The 1990s hold the most record highs of any decade (49). Newark's all-time high is 108°F, on July 22, 2011.
text.t_chg: Newark has warmed, days and nights alike
text.p_chg: Across 173 complete years: Newark's average low has risen +0.31°F per decade (95% range +0.27 to +0.34), about +5.6°F since 1844. Newark's average high has risen +0.38°F per decade (95% range +0.34 to +0.42), about +6.9°F since 1844.
text.t_mon: Lows rose in all 12 months. Highs rose in all 12 months.
text.t_rain: Rain and snow: no clear long-term change
text.p_rain: Newark's yearly precipitation shows no clear long-term change (−0.04 inches per decade, a range that includes zero). The 1991–2020 normal is 46.6 inches a year. The wettest year was 2011 (69.91 in); the driest, 1965 (26.09 in).
